summary: Cuba is the largest island country in the Caribbean. It became a socialist state after the 1959 revolution and is known for cigars, rum, classic vintage cars and its musical culture.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Diego Velázquez led the Spanish conquest of Cuba in 1511, and Catholicism became the only legal religion with colonization; the “Virgin of Charity” (Virgen de la Caridad), discovered around 1612 at Cobre in the east, later became the nation’s patron. After the 1959 revolution the government confiscated church schools and expelled large numbers of clergy, and the Church shrank for a time; in 1992 a constitutional amendment made the state secular, and after Pope John Paul II visited Cuba in 1998, religious activity gradually recovered. Today most people have been baptized, but few attend church regularly.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The revolution led by Castro in 1959 established a socialist regime, and the 1976 constitution made Marxist-Leninist atheism the state ideology, so believers were long excluded from the Communist Party and important posts. Decades of atheist education and restrictions on religious activity led many families to stop passing on faith; although the situation eased after the Communist Party opened its membership to believers in 1991, the non-religious still make up a considerable share.

ranking.name: Afro-Cuban religions (Santería, etc.)
ranking.description: From the 16th to the 19th century, hundreds of thousands of West African slaves were shipped to Cuba for the sugar plantations, many of them Yoruba, whose orisha beliefs merged with Catholic saints to form Santería (Regla de Ocha); for example, the thunder god Changó corresponds to Saint Barbara, and the love goddess Oshún to the Virgin of Charity. Those of Kongo descent developed Palo Monte. Because it can coexist with Catholicism, many people follow both, and actual participants far outnumber the statistics.

ranking.name: Protestantism
ranking.description: After the Spanish–American War of 1898 the United States occupied Cuba, and American Baptist, Methodist and Presbyterian missionaries followed, establishing schools and churches in various places. After the revolution Protestantism was likewise restricted, but during the “Special Period” economic crisis of the 1990s, Pentecostal churches centered on home gatherings grew rapidly.

religion.background: Four hundred years of Spanish colonial rule made Catholicism Cuba’s mainstream faith, while the West African slaves who were trafficked there blended Yoruba and other traditional beliefs into Catholicism, forming a distinctive Afro-Cuban religion. American influence after 1898 brought Protestantism. After the 1959 revolution the government pursued atheism, church property and schools were nationalized, and religion withdrew from public life for a long time; only when policy relaxed in the 1990s and successive popes visited did religion become active again, and today a defining feature is the coexistence of syncretic belief and non-religion.

ranking.name: Spanish
ranking.description: After the Spanish conquest in 1511, the indigenous Taíno rapidly died out from warfare, forced labor and infectious disease, and Spanish became the only common language of the entire island. Cuban Spanish was deeply influenced by immigrants from Andalusia and the Canary Islands and often swallows the s at the end of syllables; the words huracán (the source of “hurricane”) and tabaco are traces left by the Taíno language. After the revolution, the nationwide literacy campaign (1961) further consolidated the spread of standard Spanish.

ranking.name: Haitian Creole
ranking.description: With the expansion of the Cuban sugar industry in the early 20th century, large numbers of seasonal cane workers were brought in from Haiti in the 1910s and 1920s, and some put down roots in eastern provinces such as Camagüey and Ciego de Ávila, so Haitian Creole has persisted. During the Great Depression of the 1930s many Haitians were repatriated, and the descendants who remained gradually switched to Spanish; today it is used mainly by the older generation and by rural communities in the east.

language.history: Before Columbus arrived in 1492, Arawakan languages such as Taíno were spoken on the island; after colonization they vanished along with the indigenous people, leaving only loanwords such as canoa and barbacoa. Spanish became dominant from the 16th century and absorbed words from West African slave languages (such as the vocabulary of Yoruba preserved to this day in religious rituals). Haitian and Jamaican immigrants in the early 20th century brought Creole languages, and American influence left a good number of English loanwords. The revolutionary government’s literacy campaign of 1961 taught hundreds of thousands of people to read and write within a year, bringing standard Spanish deep into the whole country.

ranking.name: Ropa vieja
ranking.description: Flank steak is stewed until tender and shredded into fine strands, then simmered with a sauce (sofrito) made from tomato, onion, sweet pepper and garlic, and eaten with white rice and black beans.
ranking.history: This dish originated in the Canary Islands of Spain, where it was a frugal way of shredding and recooking the leftover meat from a stew (cocido), and it traveled to Cuba with immigrants. The name means “old clothes” because the shredded meat looks like strips of rags; a folk tale tells of a poor man who could not afford meat, threw old clothes into a pot and prayed, and they turned into a delicious stew. After the revolution the government strictly controlled cattle slaughter, and beef became especially scarce during the “Special Period” of the 1990s, making it a precious dish on the island, while it became widespread among Cuban immigrant communities in Miami and is regarded as Cuba’s national dish.

ranking.name: Moros y cristianos
ranking.description: Black beans and rice are cooked together in one pot into a dark bean rice, seasoned with onion, garlic, cumin and bay leaf, and often served as a side with roasted meat.
ranking.history: The name means “Moors and Christians,” with black beans standing for the Moors and white rice for the Christians; the allusion comes from the Reconquista on the Iberian Peninsula (711–1492), and the expression was brought by the Spanish colonists. The practice of cooking rice and beans together is related to the food traditions of West African slaves, as beans were a cheap and filling source of protein on the plantations. Today it is one of the most basic staples on the Cuban home table and is sure to appear at festive feasts.

ranking.name: Roast suckling pig (Lechón asado)
ranking.description: A whole suckling pig is marinated overnight in a mojo sauce of sour orange juice, garlic and oregano, then slow-roasted over charcoal or in a pit until the skin is crisp and the meat tender.
ranking.history: Pigs were livestock brought to the Caribbean by Spanish colonists in the 16th century and were raised in large numbers in the Cuban countryside, so whole roast pig became the most important dish for entertaining guests. The sour-orange marinade combines Spanish citrus and garlic seasoning. Cubans traditionally must have roast suckling pig at the family reunion on Christmas Eve (Nochebuena); Christmas was abolished as a holiday after 1969 and restored only in 1997, but many families privately kept the custom all along, and Cubans exiled in Miami have carried on the tradition with the “Caja China” roasting box.

ranking.name: Picadillo a la cubana
ranking.description: Ground beef is stir-fried with tomato sauce, onion and garlic, then olives, raisins and capers are added, giving a salty-sweet flavor; it is eaten with white rice and fried plantain.
ranking.history: The name comes from the Spanish “picar” (to chop); it is a home-style dish that was brought to Latin America in the Spanish colonial period, with a different version in each country. The sweet-and-salty pairing of raisins and olives can be traced to the style of the Iberian Peninsula under Islamic rule, which was influenced by Arab cuisine. Because ground meat is cheap and easy to portion, it became a common home dish in Cuba during the long years of rationing, and it is still a frequent dish on school and family tables.

ranking.name: Tostones
ranking.description: Green plantains are cut into chunks, fried, flattened, and fried a second time, making them crisp outside and fluffy inside; they are eaten sprinkled with salt or dipped in garlic mojo and are the most common side dish beside roast meats and stews.
ranking.history: The plantain originated in Southeast Asia, reached the Iberian Peninsula via Africa, and was brought to the Caribbean by the Spanish in the early 16th century, where it became an important staple for plantation slaves. The double-frying method is related to West African ways of handling starchy crops and also spread throughout the Caribbean and Latin America; the name derives from “tostar” (to toast, to fry crisp). In Cuba it is an indispensable side beside roast pork and stews and is also a common street snack, representing the blending of African and Spanish food cultures.
